newsitem.title: UK: World oil prices as volatile as the weather.
newsitem.headline: World oil prices as volatile as the weather.

text.p: World oil prices bounced around in extremely volatile trade on Thursday, in a market held to ransom by the weather, oil traders said.
London February futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend were trading down 11 cents at $23.81 a barrel at 1700 GMT, having made a brief upward spurt to $24.00 earlier.
With oil stocks running at historical lows in key western markets, prices have become ultra-sensitive to the vagaries of the elements.
"The market is fundamentally well-supported, but it can jump either way on perceptions of the weather," said Charles Gray of Prudential Bache futures brokers in London.

Bone-chilling temperatures have swept the United States this week, and forecasters are predicting more of the same with a cold front expected to hit the Midwest by early next week, pulling temperatures about ten degrees below normal.
But all eyes were on the U.S. Gulf coast refining belt in Texas and Louisiana, where refineries will have to cope with the demand surge from sub-zero temperatures which could send prices soaring.
"Because stocks are so low there's no cushion to deal with production problems or any other disruptions," an oil trader said.
As Christmas approaches and trade thins, analysts said that diminishing trading volumes are adding to the market's instability.
"A lot of people are easing out of the market so it's becoming thinner and potentially more volatile," said Gray.
Against the background of low inventories and cold weather, analysts said oil markets would have little difficulty in absorbing Iraqi crude exports under the United Nations oil-for-food agreement.
Iraq is allowed to export $2 billion of crude over six months to buy humanitarian supplies after international sanctions imposed on its invasion of Iraq halted oil sales for six years.
Seventeen companies from Europe, Russia, the United States and the Far East have already confirmed signing contracts with Baghdad for around 450,000 barrels per day of sales.

The flow of exports from Iraq is ramping up, with two tankers already loaded at the Middle East Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr and now headed across the Atlantic to the U.S. and the Caribbean, shipping sources said.

Turkey's state oil company Tupras has already bought a cargo of Iraqi crude from the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, and three more vessels with European destinations are scheduled to load up before the end of the year.
